analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare to negotiate drug prices, with compulsory licensing if companies refuse.
analysis.headline: Sen. Sherrod Brown's Medicare drug-price negotiation bill, introduced with 4 Democratic cosponsors, sat in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing, markup, or vote until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the government to negotiate drug prices for Medicare's prescription drug benefit. Today, current law explicitly forbids Medicare from negotiating with drug companies. If a company refuses to agree to a fair price, the government could license other manufacturers to make the drug for Medicare — overriding patents and exclusivities — and pay the original maker reasonable compensation. For one year, the price could also be capped at the average price charged in other wealthy countries, and if the company still refused, the license could extend to all federal health programs like Medicaid and the VA.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, who would see lower out-of-pocket drug costs as the government negotiates prices and can license cheaper copies when companies hold out. Taxpayers also benefit, since Medicare Part D is largely publicly financed and lower drug prices mean lower federal spending.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services to negotiate prices for drugs covered under Medicare's prescription drug benefit, which current law prohibits [S2].

If negotiation fails, the Secretary must license the drug's patents, clinical trial data, and other government-granted exclusivities so other manufacturers can make it for Medicare, with reasonable compensation paid to the original maker [S3].

For one year after a drug is provided under a competitive license, Medicare plans cannot pay more than the average of the drug's prices in the ten largest OECD countries, and if the maker refuses that price, the license extends to all federal health programs, including Medicaid and VA [S3].
Negotiation must weigh a drug's clinical and cost effectiveness, the financial burden on patients, unmet patient needs, and the manufacturer's global revenues and R&D investment [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, who would lose the guaranteed high Medicare prices they get under the current negotiation ban, and could see their patents and exclusivities licensed away if they refuse to deal. Taxpayers could also bear compensation payments to licensed manufacturers determined by the Court of Federal Claims.

drawbacks.text: Allowing the government to override patents and market exclusivities when negotiation fails would weaken the incentive to invest in developing new drugs, since the reward for a successful drug could be capped or licensed away [S3].

Manufacturers who lose exclusivity through licensing can seek compensation from the U.S. government in the Court of Federal Claims, so taxpayers might end up paying litigation awards even as prices fall [S3].
Basing interim prices on the average of prices in ten foreign countries could make the U.S. the low-price country and raise questions about access to very expensive new therapies.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the roughly 45 million people with Medicare drug coverage, the benefit is direct: the current law ban on negotiation is one of the main reasons Americans pay far more for the same drugs than people in other wealthy countries, and this bill attacks it with real teeth — licensing authority, not just talks. The cost is borne almost entirely by a single industry, plus possible compensation awards. The trade-off is the R&D incentive question: overriding exclusivities could slow development of future drugs, which is a real cost, though the bill's compensation mechanism is an attempt to soften it. On balance this is a high-stakes transfer of bargaining power from drug companies to patients and taxpayers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never took it up; it died there when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Sherrod Brown introduced the bill on February 7, 2019, joined by Sens. Baldwin and Klobuchar [S3].
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day; that was the last action of any kind in its two-year life [S5].
The bill had 4 cosponsors, all Democrats [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers kept the current-law prohibition on Medicare price negotiation and their monopoly pricing power in the largest U.S. drug buyer. Medicare beneficiaries continued paying the higher prices that negotiation might have lowered.

for.name: Sen. Sherrod Brown
for.role: U.S. Senator from Ohio; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill requiring Medicare drug price negotiation with competitive licensing as a backstop.

for.name: Sens. Tammy Baldwin and Amy Klobuchar
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction; the bill was introduced 'for himself, Ms. Baldwin, and Ms. Klobuchar'.

for.name: 4 Democratic senators
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; it attracted no Republican support.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee leadership (Chair Chuck Grassley, R-IA)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing, markup, or vote after referral; the committee record shows no action beyond the February 7, 2019 referral.

against.name: Pharmaceutical industry
against.what_they_did: The industry broadly opposed Medicare price negotiation legislation during this period, defending the statutory ban on negotiation that this bill would repeal.

sides.party_line_note: All five Senate supporters of the bill were Democrats, and the Republican-led Finance Committee never moved it; no Republican cosponsored it.

industries.note: The bill removes the statutory ban on Medicare negotiation and lets the government license competitors if a company refuses a fair price, directly threatening the monopoly prices drug companies charge in Medicare Part D. Their gain under the status quo comes directly out of patients' pockets and the federal budget.

Competitive licenses would open Medicare-volume manufacturing opportunities to generic and biosimilar makers, and the Secretary must fast-track their FDA applications. Their gain comes as lower prices for patients.

industries.industry: U.S. drug manufacturers prioritized for licenses
industries.note: The bill gives preference to license holders with the highest safety standards and may prioritize domestic manufacturing, steering licensed production toward U.S. plants.
